```{r vignette-options, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R", local = TRUE)
```

mostr analyses outcomes that are recorded repeatedly on an ordered scale, such
as a hospitalized patient's condition on each day, from "at home" to "dead".
It fits a *transition model*, an ordinal regression that predicts each day's
state from the previous day's state, time, treatment, and other covariates.
From the fitted model it calculates quantities that are easy to report:

- the **state occupancy probability** (SOP), the probability of being in each
  state on each day;
- the **expected time** spent in a state, or a group of states, during
  follow-up; and
- **treatment comparisons** of either, with confidence intervals.

This article runs through one small analysis from start to finish. At the
end, a list of questions points to the articles that go further.

## The data

`sim_markov()` simulates daily states from models of published trials. The
`"actt2"` model is based on the ACTT-2 trial of hospitalized adults with
COVID-19 and uses its eight-point scale:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1, 2 | Outside hospital (1: no limitation of activities) |
| 3 to 7 | In hospital, from no oxygen needed (3) to invasive ventilation (7) |
| 8 | Dead |

We simulate 250 patients followed for 28 days. `treatment_effect = log(0.7)`
means that, on any day, treated patients have 0.7 times the odds of being in
a worse state than control patients who started the day in the same state.

```{r data}
library(mostr)

trial <- sim_markov(
  "actt2",
  n_patients = 250,
  follow_up_time = 28,
  treatment_effect = log(0.7),
  seed = 2026
)
head(trial, 4)
```

The data have one row per patient and day: the patient (`id`), the day
(`time`), the state on that day (`y`), the state on the previous day
(`yprev`), and the treatment (`tx`, 0 for control and 1 for treatment). These
are the column names that mostr's functions expect by default.

Death is an *absorbing* state: a patient who dies stays dead.
`prepare_markov_data()` removes the rows after death, which carry no
information about transitions, and turns `y` and `yprev` into factors so that
each previous state gets its own coefficient.

```{r prepare}
model_data <- prepare_markov_data(trial, absorbing_state = 8)
```

## Fit a transition model

`mostm()` fits the model. The formula predicts the state from the previous
state, a smooth function of time (a restricted cubic spline with three knots,
`rms::rcs(time, 3)`), and treatment. `id_var = "id"` tells mostr which rows
belong to the same patient: it uses this to compute standard errors that
allow for the correlation between one patient's transitions, and to store
each patient's starting state for later predictions. `absorb = "8"` names
the absorbing state. The fit records it, and every later prediction keeps a
patient who reaches state 8 there. If a state occurs as an outcome but never
as a previous state and is not named in `absorb`, `mostm()` warns that it
may be absorbing.

```{r fit}
fit <- mostm(
  y ~ yprev + rms::rcs(time, 3) + tx,
  data = model_data,
  id_var = "id",
  absorb = "8"
)

exp(coef(fit)["tx"])
```

By default `mostm()` fits a proportional-odds model with `rms::orm()`. The
treatment coefficient, shown here as an odds ratio, is close to the simulated
0.7. It describes a single day's transition for patients who start that day
in the same state, which is hard to communicate. The quantities below
translate the model into the probabilities and times that patients and
clinicians care about.

## State occupancy probabilities

`avg_sops()` asks: what would the probability of each state be on each day if
every patient had received control, and if every patient had received
treatment? For each patient it sets `tx` to each value in `variables`, starts
from the patient's observed state before day 1, and chains the model's
one-day predictions forward. It then averages over the patients. Because both
arms are averaged over the same patients, the difference between them is due
to treatment alone.

- `variables = list(tx = c(0, 1))` gives the values to set;
- `times = 1:28` gives the days. SOPs are calculated one day after the other,
  so request every day, even if you only need some of them.

```{r avg-sops}
probabilities <- avg_sops(
  fit,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = 1:28
)
probabilities[probabilities$time == 28, ]
```

The result has one row per day, state, and treatment value; `estimate` is the
probability. On day 28, `r day28 <- probabilities[probabilities$time == 28 & probabilities$state == "1", ]; round(100 * day28$estimate[day28$tx == 0])`% of
patients would be outside hospital with no limitation of activities (state 1)
under control, and `r round(100 * day28$estimate[day28$tx == 1])`% under
treatment. The probabilities of the eight states add up to 1 on each day and
in each arm. `sops()` takes the same arguments and gives the probabilities of
each patient instead of their average.

## Compare treatments

`avg_comparisons()` compares the treatment values directly. The first value in
`variables` is the reference. `estimand = "time_in_state"` compares the
expected number of days spent in the states given by `state_sets`; here the
two states outside hospital. A named list labels the set in the output.

```{r compare}
days_outside <- avg_comparisons(
  fit,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  estimand = "time_in_state",
  state_sets = list(outside_hospital = c("1", "2")),
  times = 1:28
)
days_outside
```

`estimate` is the expected number of days outside hospital during the 28
days under treatment minus the number under control. With
`estimand = "sop"`, the default, `avg_comparisons()` compares the
probabilities on each day instead, and `comparison = "ratio"` gives ratios
instead of differences.

## Confidence intervals

`inferences()` adds standard errors and confidence intervals to any of these
results. `method = "delta"` calculates them from formulas (the delta method),
without random draws, so it is fast and gives the same answer every time.

```{r intervals}
days_outside_ci <- inferences(days_outside, method = "delta")
days_outside_ci[, c("estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "p.value")]
```

`conf.low` and `conf.high` are the limits of the 95% confidence interval. For
comparisons, `inferences()` also tests whether the difference is 0 and
reports the p-value.

The `vcov` argument of `inferences()` chooses which uncertainty the interval
describes:

- **Unconditional variance**, `vcov = "unconditional"`, is the default for
  averages. It accounts for the uncertainty in the estimated model
  coefficients and also for which patients happened to be sampled, and for
  their role in estimating the coefficients. The interval describes the
  average in the population that the patients come from.
- **Conditional variance**, `vcov = "conditional"`, accounts for the
  uncertainty in the coefficients but treats the patients' starting states
  and covariates as given. The interval describes the average for these
  particular patients.

The point estimate is the same either way. Here the two intervals are almost
identical; they differ more for SOPs early in follow-up, which depend
strongly on the patients' starting states.

```{r conditional}
inferences(days_outside, method = "delta", vcov = "conditional")[
  , c("estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high")
]
```

The same call adds intervals to the probabilities, and `plot_sops()` draws
them. Each panel is one state; the line type shows the treatment.

```{r plot-sops, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Eight panels, one per state, each showing the probability of that state on days 1 to 28 with a solid line for control, a dotted line for treatment and shaded 95% confidence bands. The probability of state 1 rises over follow-up and is higher under treatment, while the probabilities of the hospital states fall faster under treatment."}
probabilities_ci <- inferences(probabilities, method = "delta")

plot_sops(probabilities_ci, facet_var = "state", linetype_var = "tx") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Day", y = "State occupancy probability")
```

The delta method is available for first-order, proportional-odds models
fitted with `engine = "orm"` or `"vglm"`. For other models, `inferences()`
offers simulation (`method = "mvn"`, the default) and two kinds of bootstrap
(`method = "bootstrap"` and `method = "fwb"`).

## Where to go next

`?mostr` lists every function by task. The articles below go further.

**How do I check that the model describes the data?**
[The proportional-odds article](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/full-po-sops.html) compares observed and model-based transitions and
correlations between days with `plot_transitions()`, `plot_correlation()`,
and `plot_variogram()`.

**What if a covariate's effect differs between states?**
[The partial proportional-odds article](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/partial-po-vglm-sops.html) fits a partial proportional-odds model, in
which, for example, the effect of time on the odds of death differs from its
effect on the odds of being in hospital.

**What if today's state depends on more than yesterday's?**
[The second-order article](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/second-order-orm-sops.html) adds the state two days back.

**What if the outcome has many levels, such as a score from 1 to 30?**
[The article on many outcome levels](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/many-levels-previous-state-spline.html) models the previous state with
a spline and compares arms by time benefit.

**What if patients are seen at scheduled visits rather than every day?**
[The article on time as a factor](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/factor-time-orm-sops.html) treats each visit as a category of time and
converts the results to days with `interpolate_sops()`.

**Which confidence intervals should I use, and how are they calculated?**
[The analytical confidence intervals article](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/analytical-confidence-intervals.html) explains conditional and
unconditional variance, compares treatments for each patient with
`comparisons()`, and extracts covariances with `vcov()`.
[The article comparing MVN simulation and the bootstrap](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/mvn-vs-bootstrap-orm-sops.html) and
[the fractional weighted bootstrap article](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/fractional-weighted-bootstrap-sops.html) cover simulation and the
bootstrap, including comparisons within subgroups.

**How do I fit a Bayesian model?**
[The Bayesian article](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/bayesian-rmsb-sops.html) uses `engine = "blrm"`, whose results carry
posterior intervals without an `inferences()` step.

The package website answers
[frequently asked questions](https://scjohannes.github.io/mostr/articles/faq.html),
including common error messages.
